Mortgagee shall give Mortgagor not less than fifteen (15) days' prior written notice of any such selection and conforming changes, and any such replacement shall be effected by an amendment to the Note executed by Mortgagor and Mortgagee; if Mortgagor fails to execute such amendment within ten (10) days after request, Mortgagee may make the replacement effective by written notice to Mortgagor, and Mortgagor shall be bound thereby.

**15.12 Statements of Account.** Mortgagee shall deliver to Mortgagor, upon Mortgagor's written request not more frequently than once per calendar quarter, a statement of the outstanding principal balance, accrued interest and other amounts due under the Loan. Mortgagee's books and records shall be presumptively correct absent manifest error.

# ARTICLE 16 — PREPAYMENT

**16.1 Lockout Period — No Prepayment.** The Loan may not be prepaid in whole or in part at any time during the Lockout Period (the period from the Closing Date through the day immediately preceding the twenty-fourth (24th) monthly anniversary of the date of the Note). No voluntary prepayment of principal shall be permitted during the Lockout Period, and any attempted prepayment during the Lockout Period shall be void and of no effect and shall not discharge or reduce the Indebtedness; *provided* that the foregoing shall not limit the application of insurance proceeds or Condemnation awards in accordance with **Article 14**, which shall be applied at par without any prepayment premium, penalty or Yield Maintenance Premium.

**16.2 Yield Maintenance Period.** From the expiration of the Lockout Period through the forty-eighth (48th) monthly anniversary of the date of the Note (the "**Yield Maintenance Period**"), the Loan may be prepaid in whole, but not in part, upon not less than thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Mortgagee, and upon payment, in addition to all other amounts due, of a prepayment premium (the "**Yield Maintenance Premium**") equal to the greater of:

> **(a)** one percent (1.00%) of the principal amount of the Loan being prepaid; and
>
> **(b)** the excess, if any, of (i) the present value, discounted monthly at the Treasury Rate, of the aggregate interest that would have accrued on the principal amount being prepaid during the period from the date of prepayment through the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, computed at the rate per annum equal to the Note rate in effect on the date of prepayment, over (ii) the present value, discounted monthly at the Treasury Rate, of the aggregate interest that would have accrued on such principal amount during the same period, computed at a rate per annum equal to the Treasury Rate plus fifty (50) basis points (0.50%);
>
> *provided* that the amount determined under this clause (b) shall in no event be less than zero, and shall be zero if the Note rate in effect on the date of prepayment is less than or equal to the Treasury Rate plus fifty (50) basis points.

For purposes of this Section 16.2: (i) the "**Treasury Rate**" means the yield to maturity, as of the second (2nd) Business Day preceding the date of prepayment, of the United States Treasury security having a maturity date closest to, but not exceeding, the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, as reported in Federal Reserve Statistical Release H.15 — Selected Interest Rates (or any successor publication) under the heading "Treasury Constant Maturities"; if the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period does not correspond exactly to a published maturity, the Treasury Rate shall be determined by linear interpolation between the yields reported for the two nearest published maturities (or, if the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period is later than the longest published maturity, the yield on the longest published maturity); (ii) discounting shall be computed monthly using a periodic rate equal to the Treasury Rate divided by twelve (12) and the number of whole and partial months remaining in the Yield Maintenance Period; (iii) if the Treasury Rate is not published for the applicable date, the Treasury Rate shall be determined on the basis of the most recent publication available, as reasonably determined by Mortgagee; and (iv) Mortgagee's computation of the Yield Maintenance Premium shall be conclusive absent manifest error and shall be set forth in a written calculation delivered to Mortgagor not less than five (5) Business Days prior to the date of prepayment.

**16.3 Open Prepayment Period.** During the final twelve (12) months of the term of the Loan (that is, from and after the forty-eighth (48th) monthly anniversary of the date of the Note through the Maturity Date), the Loan may be prepaid in whole or in part at any time and from time to time, without payment of any prepayment premium, penalty or yield maintenance amount, upon not less than fifteen (15) days' prior written notice to Mortgagee.

**16.4 Mechanics of Prepayment.** Each notice of prepayment shall be in writing, shall be irrevocable, shall specify the date and amount of the prepayment, and shall be accompanied by the payment, on the date specified, of the principal amount being prepaid together with all accrued and unpaid interest on the amount prepaid, the Yield Maintenance Premium (if applicable), the Late Charge and all other amounts then due under the Loan Documents. No prepayment shall be made on a date other than a Payment Date, and no partial prepayment shall be permitted during the Lockout Period or the Yield Maintenance Period. Any partial prepayment permitted under **Section 16.3** shall be in a minimum amount of $500,000 and in increments of $100,000 in excess thereof. All partial prepayments shall be applied to the installments of principal in the inverse order of their maturity, shall not reduce the amount of any monthly installment of principal and interest, shall not change the amortization schedule, and shall not change the Maturity Date.

**16.5 Involuntary Prepayments.** Any application of insurance proceeds or Condemnation awards to the Indebtedness under **Article 14**, and any application of Escrow Funds, Rents or other Collateral to the Indebtedness at any time when no Event of Default has occurred and is continuing, shall be made at par, without any prepayment premium, penalty or Yield Maintenance Premium.

**16.6 Prepayment After Acceleration.** If Mortgagee accelerates the Indebtedness following an Event of Default and Mortgagor tenders payment of the entire Indebtedness, the Yield Maintenance Premium (computed as if the payment were a voluntary prepayment on the date of tender) shall be due and payable to the extent permitted by applicable law. Mortgagor acknowledges that the Yield Maintenance Premium is bargained-for consideration for the Loan and is not a penalty, and Mortgagor waives any right to assert that the Yield Maintenance Premium is unenforceable as a penalty, forfeiture or liquidated damages provision, except to the extent such waiver is prohibited by applicable law.

**16.7 Nature of Premium.** Mortgagor acknowledges that (a) the Yield Maintenance Premium is intended to compensate Mortgagee for the loss of its investment yield caused by an early repayment of the Loan; (b) the amount of such loss is difficult and impractical to ascertain and depends upon the movement of interest rates and market conditions after the date of this Mortgage; (c) the formula set forth in **Section 16.2** is a reasonable, objective, mathematically determinate method of estimating such loss; and (d) the Yield Maintenance Premium is not a penalty or a liquidated damages provision, but is consideration for the making of the Loan.

**Part 1 — The Land Use Restriction**

The land use restriction and institutional control recorded in Deed Book 1203 at Page 89, RMC Office for Charleston County, South Carolina, was imposed by SCDHEC as a condition of its No Further Action determination dated August 12, 2021 for SCDHEC Site ID SC-29403-0772, relating to a historical release of perchloroethylene and petroleum-based solvents from the former dry-cleaning operation at the adjoining property municipally known as 518 King Street. The Land Use Restriction runs with the land and binds all current and future owners, tenants, lessees, successors and assigns of Lot 7 (Tax Map No. 460-12-04-007). It imposes two obligations:

| Requirement | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **(a) Prohibition on residential use** | The ground floor of Lot 7 (comprising Bay 1, 520 King Street, approximately 3,800 square feet) shall not be converted to or used for residential purposes. Current use as a specialty grocery is consistent with the restriction. |
| **(b) Vapor barrier maintenance** | The owner must maintain, in good condition and working order, the vapor barrier system installed beneath the concrete floor slab of Bay 1. The vapor barrier shall not be penetrated, removed or compromised without SCDHEC's prior written approval. Any renovation, construction, demolition or alteration affecting the Bay 1 floor slab must include inspection and, if necessary, repair or replacement of the vapor barrier, with prior written notification to SCDHEC. |

The No Further Action determination is contingent upon continued compliance with these institutional controls. Non-compliance may result in SCDHEC reopening the site for additional investigation, remediation or other regulatory action at the expense of the then-current owner.

| 6 | Annual certificate of Mortgagor and compliance report of a licensed environmental professional confirming no residential use, barrier integrity, full compliance with the Land Use Restriction and no notice of violation or site reopening | Annually within 30 days after year end | Section 7.6(c)(vii); Section 7.9(g) |

# EXHIBIT E — SCDHEC LAND USE RESTRICTION AND COMPLIANCE PROTOCOL

**Part 1 — The Land Use Restriction**

The land use restriction and institutional control recorded in Deed Book 1203 at Page 89, RMC Office for Charleston County, South Carolina, was imposed by SCDHEC as a condition of its No Further Action determination dated August 12, 2021 for SCDHEC Site ID SC-29403-0772, relating to a historical release of perchloroethylene and petroleum-based solvents from the former dry-cleaning operation at the adjoining property municipally known as 518 King Street. The Land Use Restriction runs with the land and binds all current and future owners, tenants, lessees, successors and assigns of Lot 7 (Tax Map No. 460-12-04-007). It imposes two obligations:

| Requirement | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **(a) Prohibition on residential use** | The ground floor of Lot 7 (comprising Bay 1, 520 King Street, approximately 3,800 square feet) shall not be converted to or used for residential purposes. Current use as a specialty grocery is consistent with the restriction. |
| **(b) Vapor barrier maintenance** | The owner must maintain, in good condition and working order, the vapor barrier system installed beneath the concrete floor slab of Bay 1. The vapor barrier shall not be penetrated, removed or compromised without SCDHEC's prior written approval. Any renovation, construction, demolition or alteration affecting the Bay 1 floor slab must include inspection and, if necessary, repair or replacement of the vapor barrier, with prior written notification to SCDHEC. |

The No Further Action determination is contingent upon continued compliance with these institutional controls. Non-compliance may result in SCDHEC reopening the site for additional investigation, remediation or other regulatory action at the expense of the then-current owner.

| 2 | Qualified, licensed environmental professional to inspect and confirm the integrity of the vapor barrier beneath the Bay 1 slab | Prior to, or promptly following, closing | Section 7.6(c)(vii) |

| 6 | Annual certificate of Mortgagor and compliance report of a licensed environmental professional confirming no residential use, barrier integrity, full compliance with the Land Use Restriction and no notice of violation or site reopening | Annually within 30 days after year end | Section 7.6(c)(vii); Section 7.9(g) |

::: {custom-style="Title"}
MEMORANDUM
:::

::: {custom-style="Subtitle"}
FIELDING, ASHWORTH & COLE LLP — Charleston | Savannah

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT — PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION AND FOR THE PURPOSE OF PROVIDING LEGAL ADVICE**
:::

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **TO:** | Catherine "Kit" Ashworth, Partner, Real Estate Practice Group Chair |
| **FROM:** | Jordan Vickers, Associate |
| **CC:** | File |
| **DATE:** | March 28, 2025 |
| **RE:** | First draft — Mortgage and Security Agreement (Calverley Heritage Bank / Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC; CHB Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047; 520–534 King Street, Charleston, South Carolina) — reserved issues, cross-document inconsistencies and instructions required |

# 1. PURPOSE, SCOPE AND METHOD

**1.1 Purpose.** This memorandum transmits and explains the first draft of the Mortgage and Security Agreement (the "**Mortgage**") for the captioned transaction and identifies the issues that require your decision, the client's decision or further information before the draft is released to Marcus Prideaux on April 1 and before closing. It responds, section by section, to your markup notes of March 18, 2025 (the "**Markup Notes**") and records every point at which I departed from those notes and why.

**1.2 Method.** I read each source document in full, built a source-to-issue log, and independently recomputed every total, percentage, date interval, threshold and cross-reference used in the draft rather than relying on the figures stated in the record. **Section 6** contains that verification log in tabular form. Where the record conflicts, I have drafted to the executed Term Sheet (which is the binding commitment as between the parties and which provides, in Section 14.3, that in the event of conflict the Loan Documents control) and have flagged the conflict here rather than resolving it unilaterally.

**1.3 Source documents reviewed.** 

| Key | Document | Date | Status / limitation |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **TS** | Executed Term Sheet — Commercial Real Estate Loan, Deal Reference CHB CRE Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047 | April 1, 2025 | Executed by Lender, Borrower and Guarantor; binding commitment |
| **TC** | Commitment for Title Insurance No. PT-2025-04-1178, Commonwealth National Title Underwriters Inc. through Prestige Title & Settlement Services LLC | Effective Feb. 28, 2025 | Commitment only; expires Aug. 28, 2025; subject to Schedule B-I requirements |
| **APP** | Summary Appraisal Report, Pinnacle Valuation Services LLC, File No. PVS-2025-0214-CHS | Feb. 14, 2025 | Summary (not complete) report; as-stabilized value is a prospective value subject to a hypothetical condition |
| **ESA** | Phase I Environmental Site Assessment Executive Summary, Clearfield Environmental Consulting LLC, Report No. CLR-2025-0119 | Jan. 28, 2025 | Executive summary only; expressly states it "does not constitute a complete Phase I" |
| **KAM** | Your internal markup notes to me | Mar. 18, 2025 | Instructions |
| **OA** | Redacted Summary of Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC (Cartwright & Lyons LLP) | Jan. 12, 2024, as amended through Mar. 1, 2025 | **Redacted summary only** — not the full operating agreement; expressly insufficient to confirm SPE compliance |
| **RR** | Rent Roll and Lease Abstracts (workbook, with Summary, Lease Abstracts and Vacancy Schedule tabs) | Rent roll dated Mar. 1, 2025 | Abstracts only; underlying leases not produced |
| **RBS** | Renovation Budget and Draw Schedule (workbook, with Budget Detail and Draw Schedule tabs) | Undated; prepared by or for Borrower | Borrower-prepared; internally inconsistent as noted at **A-6** |

**1.4 Documents not in the record.** The following are referenced in the record but were not available for this draft, and the corresponding provisions are drafted on assumptions that must be conformed on receipt: the Promissory Note (**H-1**); the Guaranty Agreement, Completion Guaranty and Environmental Indemnity Agreement; the executed construction contract with Beaufort Builders Group LLC (**H-1**); the ALTA/NSPS Survey dated January 15, 2025; the full unredacted operating agreement and the March 1, 2025 amendment (**D-8**); the underlying leases (**F-1**); the SCDHEC remediation file for Site ID SC-29403-0772 (**C-3**); and the closing statement / sources-and-uses (**A-4**).

**1.5 Priority definitions.** Throughout this memorandum: **Priority 1** = must be resolved (or expressly reserved to the client in writing) before the draft is released and before any reliance is placed on the affected provision; **Priority 2** = must be resolved before closing; **Priority 3** = negotiation or monitoring point.

# 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY — TOP-RISK REGISTER

Twelve issues carry most of the risk in this transaction. Each is developed in the body of this memorandum at the cross-reference shown.

| # | Issue | Priority | Where developed |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | **DSCR covenant is unachievable on the record.** Even at the borrower's own "stabilized best case," NOI of $622,772 supports a DSCR of only 0.72x on interest-only debt service and 0.55x on amortizing debt service, against a 1.25x covenant tested from month 24 — the same month amortization begins. The loan would have to be approximately $6.5 million to test at 1.25x. | 1 | **A-2** |
| 2 | **Occupancy is 56.13%, not 68%.** Both the Term Sheet and the appraisal overstate occupied area (21,400 SF against an actual 17,400 SF); the two figures in the Term Sheet are internally inconsistent. Every occupancy-driven covenant, budget and lease-up assumption built on 68% is overstated. | 1 | **A-1** |
| 3 | **Borrower's operating agreement does not support the SPE structure.** No independent manager, no separateness covenants, no single-purpose purpose clause, no lender consent to dissolution or amendment, and bankruptcy is not a "Major Decision." The Mortgage as drafted represents that the agreement has been amended; that representation is not yet true. | 1 | **D-1**, **D-2** |
| 4 | **The yield maintenance formula in the Markup Notes does not work and conflicts with the Term Sheet.** As literally drafted it produces a negative number for a partially amortizing loan (there is no scheduled balloon at month 48 to compare against). I have drafted the Term Sheet formulation instead, which produces a premium; the 50 basis points must be placed correctly. | 1 | **E-1** to **E-4** |
| 5 | **Sources and uses do not balance.** Loan plus equity equals $20,950,000, which is exactly purchase price plus renovation budget — leaving no identified source for closing costs (origination fee $147,500, mortgage recording tax $54,575, plus title, survey, legal, appraisal and ESA costs) or for the $150,000 TI/LC reserve required at closing. Identified shortfall: at least $352,075. | 1 | **A-4** |
| 6 | **Anson Lane chain of title.** Title derives from a quitclaim deed; the Title Commitment does not except the parcel but the Title Insurer's addendum expressly disclaims that the chain is "equivalent to that of Parcel One." Coverage must be affirmatively confirmed and endorsed before closing. | 1 | **B-1** |
| 7 | **Lowcountry Provisions lease is silent on assignment, estoppel and SNDA.** The tenant has no contractual obligation to deliver the estoppel or SNDA that Section 12.1(j)–(k) of the Term Sheet makes a condition precedent to closing. | 1 | **F-1**, **B-9** |
| 8 | **Environmental covenants must be specific, and the Markup Notes understate the requirement.** The Title Insurer's special instruction to closer and Section 5.4 of the Term Sheet require the Mortgage itself to covenant compliance with the SCDHEC land use restriction, address vapor-barrier maintenance and inspection, and create an Event of Default. A "standard template" covenant is not sufficient. | 1 | **C-1**, **C-2** |
| 9 | **Environmental default trigger interacts with the renovation.** Façade restoration and other work near Bay 1 could compromise the vapor barrier; the draft conditions Draws on SCDHEC notice and pre/post-work environmental certification. The construction contract does not yet contain the required covenant. | 1 | **C-2** |
| 10 | **Direct and indirect transfer restrictions conflict with the operating agreement.** The operating agreement permits Tidewater to transfer its 18% interest to any "successor fund" without consent, and permits upstream change of control of GDG; Section 10.3 of the Term Sheet permits neither. Conforming amendment and member joinders are required. | 2 | **D-3**, **D-4**, **D-5** |
| 11 | **Guaranty support has a ten-month hole.** The interest-shortfall guaranty covers only the first 14 months; DSCR testing begins at month 24; there is no debt service reserve, no cash sweep and no DSCR cure right. Months 15–24 are unguarded and untested — and that is precisely when lease-up risk concentrates. | 1 | **G-1**, **G-3**, **G-8** |
| 12 | **Title and closing mechanics are time-critical.** The survey is dated January 15, 2025 and must be re-certified to a date within 90 days of closing — April 15 is exactly day 90. The Title Commitment expires August 28, 2025; the Term Sheet closing deadline is May 15, 2025. Recording order (deed then Mortgage) and the future-advance endorsement must be sequenced. | 2 | **B-4**, **B-5**, **B-6**, **B-8** |

**The four issues I would raise with Marcus Prideaux first.** (i) The DSCR covenant cannot be satisfied under the structure as committed (**A-2**); the client needs to decide whether the covenant is to be retained as drafted, re-tested on a different basis, supported by a DSCR cure deposit, or whether the loan is re-sized. (ii) The sources-and-uses gap (**A-4**) is a closing risk, not merely a documentation point. (iii) The SPE amendments (**D-1**) must be signed by all three members, and we do not yet know whether Tidewater's general partner and Harborline can bind their respective entities. (iv) The prepayment formula (**E-1**) is the only place where the instrument as drafted departs materially from your instructions, and the client should confirm the economic result.

# 3. RESPONSE TO YOUR MARKUP NOTES

**3.1 Recitals and defined terms (your §1).** Implemented as instructed. Recitals A–F reference each Loan Document by name; "Initial Advance" ($12,500,000) and "Renovation Holdback" ($2,250,000) are separately defined, with the holdback disbursement conditions at **Article 10**; "Property" captures all three tax parcels and the vacated Anson Lane strip; "Loan Documents" cross-references the GC Contract, the Approved Renovation Budget and each reserve arrangement (defined term "Loan Documents" and **Article 2**); "Guarantor" and "Maturity Date" as instructed. I added a recital (**Recital E**) describing the Controlled Recognized Environmental Condition and the Land Use Restriction, because the environmental covenants in **Section 7.6** need a factual anchor in the instrument that will be recorded.

**3.2 Granting clause and Anson Lane (your §2).** The granting clause covers the fee estate, Improvements, fixtures and systems, personal property, accounts and reserves, proceeds and awards, permits and entitlements, contracts (expressly including the GC Contract), Leases and Rents, books and records, tax refunds and proceeds (**Section 2.1(a)–(l)**). All three tax map numbers and the Anson Lane strip appear in the granting clause itself and in Exhibit A, as you directed. The legal description is in **Exhibit A** by incorporation and is flagged on its face as requiring insertion of the surveyor's metes and bounds description before recording.

On the **Anson Lane chain of title**, I have not been able to resolve the concern you raised. The Title Commitment does **not** except the strip from Schedule B-II — which is helpful — but the vesting addendum disclaims any representation that the chain "is equivalent to that of Parcel One," and Note 3 to closer reserves premium and may limit coverage by endorsement. The Mortgage therefore requires recordation of a full metes and bounds description, requires Mortgagee's approval of the Title Policy as issued, and I have built the endorsement requirement into the defined term "Title Policy." This is developed at **B-1**. I have **not** been able to confirm requirement (2) of your note (complete and unbroken vesting chain from the City of Charleston) because the municipal records and recorded ordinance are not in our file; that is an open item at **Section 7**.

**3.3 Assignment of leases, rents and profits (your §3).** Implemented as an **absolute and present assignment** in **Article 5**, with the words "collateral" and "as additional security" eliminated throughout. The provision states that the assignment is absolute and present, effective on execution without regard to any default, includes the representation that Mortgagor has the right to assign "specifically and without limitation" the Lowcountry Provisions lease (**Section 5.2(e)**), grants a revocable license to collect until default (**Section 5.3**), permits collection upon written notice to tenants without a court order or receiver (**Section 5.4**), includes the receiver mechanism you asked for (**Section 13.3**), and adds the post-closing covenant to obtain a conforming amendment at the next renewal, extension or amendment opportunity, with the March 31, 2027 renewal-notice deadline fixed as the outside date (**Section 5.6**). Three points require your attention: the statutory citation (**F-1**), the characterization risk that an absolute assignment creates in a borrower bankruptcy (**F-4**), and the fact that the tenant has no obligation to deliver the estoppel you want (**F-1**).

**3.4 Single-purpose entity covenants (your §4).** Implemented as instructed: the Mortgage contains full SPE and separateness covenants (**Section 7.4(a)–(k)**) and a representation that the operating agreement contains the required independent-manager, separateness, single-purpose and anti-amendment provisions (**Section 6.12**). I did **not** treat that representation as a formality — on the record it is presently inaccurate (**D-1**), and I have made the executed operating agreement amendment, together with the written consent and joinder of all three members, an express condition to the truth of the representation so that the representation cannot be given falsely at closing without a visible failure of a closing condition.

**3.5 Prepayment and yield maintenance (your §5).** **This is the one place where I did not follow your instruction, and I need your direction.** Your suggested formula compares the present value of remaining scheduled payments to the principal being prepaid and floors the premium at zero. For a loan that amortizes over 25 years but matures at month 60, there is no scheduled balloon payment at the end of the Yield Maintenance Period, so the present value of the remaining installments (roughly $1.63 million at month 30) can never approach the outstanding principal (roughly $14.62 million). Your formula therefore yields **zero** in every realistic scenario — it would eliminate the prepayment premium entirely. I have instead drafted the Term Sheet formulation (greater of 1.00% of the prepaid principal or the present value of the interest differential), which is mathematically determinate, produces a premium, and is faithful to the binding commitment. The full analysis, including a worked example and the treatment of the 50 basis points, is at **E-1** to **E-4**.

**3.6 Other sections (your §6).** UCC collateral and fixture filing (**Article 3**), renovation disbursements (**Article 10**, with 10 business days' notice, architect certification, lien waivers at your $25,000 threshold, title date-down, inspection and 10% retainage), insurance (**Article 8**, carrying your amounts plus builder's risk and, as an addition, business income/rent loss coverage — see **H-5**), financial covenants (**Section 7.8**), default and remedies (**Articles 12–13**, with an express statement at **Section 13.2** that the Mortgage grants no power of sale and that foreclosure is judicial only), governing law and recording (**Section 18.5**, with the mortgage recording tax computed at $54,575), and environmental covenants (**Section 7.6**). On the last: your note says the standard template environmental covenant "should suffice." **I have not followed that instruction**, because the Title Insurer's Note 1 to closer and Section 5.4 of the Term Sheet both require specific covenants and a dedicated default trigger; this is developed at **C-1**.

# 4. DETAILED ISSUES AND RECOMMENDED RESOLUTIONS

## A. ECONOMIC AND UNDERWRITING ISSUES

**A-1 — Occupancy is 56.13%, not 68% (Priority 1).** The Term Sheet (§2.3) states "current occupancy is approximately sixty-eight percent (68%)" and, in the same section, that vacant space totals "13,600 square feet, or approximately 43.9% of total building area." Those two statements cannot both be true: 13,600 ÷ 31,000 = 43.87% vacancy, i.e. **56.13% occupancy**. The appraisal (APP §1 and §3.1) repeats the error and compounds it, stating "68% (21,400 SF of 31,000 SF occupied)" and "vacant area is 13,600 SF (32%)" — the occupied and vacant figures sum to 35,000 SF for a 31,000 SF building. The rent roll is correct: Bay 1 (3,800) + Bay 3 (3,800) + Suite A (9,800) = **17,400 SF occupied**, 13,600 SF vacant, 3 of 5 units. The appraisal's weighted average in-place rent of $19.40/SF is also derived from the erroneous 21,400 SF denominator; the correct figure is $23.86/SF ($415,100 ÷ 17,400).

*Effect.* Every covenant, budget, lease-up projection and stabilization assumption in the record that was calibrated to 68% occupancy is calibrated to a number that is 11.9 percentage points too high. The appraiser's as-stabilized value assumes 95% occupancy and a 18–24 month lease-up; measured from 56.13% rather than 68%, the required absorption is materially greater.

*Resolution.* The Mortgage does not state an occupancy percentage (deliberately — the instrument should not hard-code a figure that the record gets wrong). Exhibit D states 56.13% and 17,400 SF. Recommend: (i) the closing rent roll be re-certified on the correct basis; (ii) the appraisal be reviewed with the appraiser as to the occupancy error and its effect, if any, on the 6.25% as-is capitalization rate and the $18,200,000 as-is value — if the error is confined to the summary narrative the value may be unaffected, but the client should not accept the report without asking; and (iii) if the client intends any occupancy-based covenant (e.g. a lease-up benchmark or a guaranty burn-off), it must be drafted from 56.13%.

**A-2 — The DSCR covenant cannot be satisfied (Priority 1).** This is the most serious issue in the transaction. Section 7.1 of the Term Sheet sets a 1.25x minimum DSCR, tested quarterly from month 24; Section 11.1(i) makes two consecutive quarters below 1.25x an Event of Default. Section 3.9 of the Term Sheet ends the interest-only period at month 24 and starts 25-year amortization at month 25. So the first test dates coincide exactly with a step-up in debt service. Computed at the SOFR floor (3.00% + 2.85% = 5.85%), the numbers are:

| Measure | Amount |
|:---|---:|
| Monthly interest-only payment | $71,906.25 |
| Annual debt service, interest-only | $862,875 |
| Monthly P&I, 25-year amortization at 5.85% | $93,686.61 |
| Annual debt service, first amortizing year | $1,124,239 |
| NOI required for 1.25x on interest-only debt service | $1,078,594 |
| NOI required for 1.25x on amortizing debt service | $1,405,299 |
| Borrower's "stabilized best case" NOI (RR, Vacancy Schedule) | $622,772 |
| Implied DSCR on interest-only debt service | **0.72x** |
| Implied DSCR on amortizing debt service | **0.55x** |
| Borrower's "realistic" NOI at the April 15, 2027 test date | $314,782 |
| Implied DSCR on interest-only / amortizing debt service | **0.37x / 0.28x** |

Put differently: on the borrower's own stabilized projections, the loan would have to be approximately **$6.5 million** (amortizing) or **$8.5 million** (interest-only) to test at 1.25x. The loan is $14,750,000. The borrower's own workbook says the same thing in terms ("*** DOES NOT MEET 1.25x COVENANT ***").

*Resolution (client decision required).* The Mortgage implements the Term Sheet faithfully (**Sections 7.8(a), 12.1(i)**) because we cannot unilaterally rewrite a covenant the client has committed to. But I recommend we put four options to Marcus: (i) retain the covenant and accept that default is effectively pre-ordained at month 24 (not recommended — a covenant that cannot be met is a covenant that will be waived, and waiver creates lender-liability and documentation exposure); (ii) extend the interest-only period to month 36 and begin testing at month 36 to permit lease-up (addresses timing but not the arithmetic); (iii) retain the covenant and require a DSCR cure deposit, cash sweep trigger at 1.10x, or an additional interest/DSCR guaranty sized to the gap (**G-8**); or (iv) re-size the loan. This should not be left to closing.

**A-3 — As-is LTV of 81.04% requires a documented credit exception (Priority 2).** $14,750,000 ÷ $18,200,000 = 81.04%; the as-stabilized LTV of 62.77% is the more comfortable number but rests on a **prospective** value subject to a hypothetical condition (renovation complete plus 95% occupancy). Loan-to-cost is 70.41% ($14,750,000 ÷ $20,950,000) and borrower equity is 29.59% of total project cost. As you anticipated in your closing note, an 81% as-is LTV is outside conventional commercial real estate limits. *Resolution:* obtain written confirmation from Marcus that loan committee or the board has approved the exception, and place the confirmation in the closing file; if the approval is conditional, the conditions need to be reflected in the Loan Documents. I have flagged this in the Mortgage's recitals indirectly (the Loan is made "on the terms and subject to the conditions set forth in the Term Sheet") but a credit exception is not a document term and should be evidenced separately.

**A-4 — Sources and uses do not balance; identified shortfall of at least $352,075 (Priority 1).** The Term Sheet (Exhibit B) funds the renovation as $2,250,000 holdback plus $900,000 borrower equity, and the purchase price (Section 3.2) as $17,800,000. Its "Total Project Cost" (Section 3.4) is $20,950,000, exactly equal to the $14,750,000 loan plus the $6,200,000 equity commitment. But total project cost excludes closing costs and the $150,000 TI/LC reserve that Section 6.3 requires to be deposited **at closing**. Working backwards: purchase price $17,800,000 less Initial Advance $12,500,000 = $5,300,000 to come from equity; equity commitment $6,200,000 less $5,300,000 = $900,000, which is exactly the "Borrower Equity for Renovation" in the Term Sheet's Exhibit B. The equity is therefore fully committed with nothing left for closing costs or the reserve. Known closing costs alone (origination fee $147,500 plus mortgage recording tax $54,575) are $202,075, and adding the $150,000 reserve gives **$352,075** before any title premium, survey, appraisal, ESA, legal fees or documentary stamps on the deed.

*Resolution.* Require a certified closing statement and a sources-and-uses schedule as a condition precedent (already contemplated by Term Sheet §12.1(m), which requires "evidence of the funding" of the $6,200,000), and require written evidence that Borrower will fund the shortfall from additional equity or member capital contributions. Draft consequence: **Section 10.6** obliges Mortgagor to fund all costs in excess of the Renovation Holdback from its own funds, and **Section 7.4(g)** requires adequate capitalization — but neither cures a shortfall at the closing table.

**A-5 — The borrower's debt service arithmetic is wrong (Priority 3).** The rent roll's Vacancy Schedule states a monthly P&I payment of $93,500 and annual interest-only debt service of $863,375. The correct figures are **$93,686.61** (25-year, 5.85%) and **$862,875** (5.85% on $14,750,000). The errors are small ($186.61 per month; $500 per year) and run in opposite directions, but they are symptomatic of a model that has not been independently checked, which matters because the client is being asked to rely on the same model for the lease-up and NOI projections at **A-2**.

**A-6 — The renovation draw schedule does not foot to the budget (Priority 2).** The Draw Schedule tab totals **$905,000** of Borrower Equity against a $900,000 commitment (leaving a negative "$-5,000 remaining" in month 14) and **$3,155,000** of cumulative cost against a $3,150,000 budget, while its own TOTAL row asserts $900,000 and $3,150,000. Separately, the Budget Detail tab footnote says the GC Contract "exceeds Lender Holdback of $2,250,000 by $600,000" — but $150,000 of the holdback is allocated to soft costs outside the GC Contract, so the shortfall to be funded by equity on the hard-cost scope is **$750,000** ($2,850,000 less $2,100,000), not $600,000. Neither error changes the borrower's total obligation, but both obscure the funding sequence. I have conformed **Exhibit C** to the $2,250,000/$900,000/$3,150,000 figures and noted the discrepancy on the face of the exhibit, and **Section 10.2(d)** imposes a pro-rata funding test so that Lender does not fund ahead of equity.

**A-7 — Front-loaded lender funding (Priority 3).** The Draw Schedule has Lender funding $190,000 in months 1–2 against $165,000 of borrower equity, and by month 3 Lender has drawn $440,000 against $265,000 of equity (62.4% lender share against a 71.43% entitlement — so equity, not lender, is actually ahead in dollar terms, but only because of the soft-cost allocation). The Term Sheet contains no equity-first requirement. **Section 10.2(d)** adds a pro-rata test as a condition to each Draw. This is an addition to the Term Sheet and is analysed at **H-5**.

**A-8 — Balloon and rollover risk at maturity (Priority 3).** The Loan amortizes over 25 years but matures at month 60, so approximately **$13,895,165** will be outstanding at the April 15, 2030 Maturity Date (36 amortizing payments having been made). Refinance risk is compounded by rollover: the Tidemark lease (9,800 SF, 31.6% of the building and the anchor cash flow) expires **March 31, 2029**, roughly twelve and a half months before maturity, and the Lowcountry Provisions lease expires December 31, 2027. At maturity, absent renewal, the lender is looking at a substantially vacant building. Recommend the client consider a maturity-extension/rollover reserve or a cash-management trigger in the final 24 months; neither is in the Term Sheet, so this is a credit recommendation only.

## B. COLLATERAL AND TITLE ISSUES

**B-1 — Anson Lane strip: quitclaim vesting and disclaimed equivalence (Priority 1).** The strip was conveyed by **quitclaim deed** recorded in Deed Book 1128, Page 443 (TC Schedule A §3; ESA §2). The Title Commitment does not except the parcel from Schedule B-II, which is the outcome we wanted. However the vesting addendum states that the Company's willingness to insure the parcel "should not be construed as a representation that the chain of title for this parcel is equivalent to that of Parcel One," and Note 3 to closer reserves the right to require additional premium for extended coverage and/or to limit coverage by endorsement. Your three questions therefore stand as follows: (1) **fee simple insured without carve-out** — not yet confirmed; the commitment insures fee simple but the note preserves the right to limit; (2) **unbroken vesting chain from the City** — not confirmable from our file; the municipal ordinance and City records are not in the record; (3) **endorsement** — I recommend an ALTA Endorsement 34 (Identified Exception) or specific affirmative coverage for the strip rather than an ALTA 9 (which addresses restrictive covenants and encroachments, not defective vesting), and I have made the endorsement set part of the defined term "Title Policy." *Action:* I will write to Rebecca Hargrove at Prestige Title today, copy you, asking for written confirmation that the strip will be insured in fee simple without carve-out and quoting the premium for affirmative coverage, and obtain the recorded Ordinance No. 2019-084 and the City's chain from the RMC Office. ## E. PREPAYMENT AND YIELD MAINTENANCE ISSUES

**E-1 — The formula in the Markup Notes produces a zero premium; I have drafted a different formula (Priority 1).** Your §5 draft provides that the premium equals the positive excess of "(A) the present value of all remaining scheduled monthly payments of interest and principal from the prepayment date through the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period … over (B) the outstanding principal amount being prepaid," floored at zero. Applied to this Loan, the result is not a small premium — it is a large negative number:

| Element (illustrative prepayment at month 30; 18 months remaining; 25-year amortization) | Amount |
|:---|---:|
| Outstanding principal at month 30 | $14,617,715 |
| Present value of the 18 remaining scheduled P&I installments, discounted at a 4.00% Treasury rate | $1,634,124 |
| Excess of (A) over (B) | **$(12,983,591)** — i.e. zero premium |

The defect is structural, not arithmetical: with 25-year amortization and a 60-month maturity, **there is no scheduled balloon payment at the end of the Yield Maintenance Period**, so the stream of "remaining scheduled monthly payments" never includes repayment of principal. A formula of this kind works only for a fully amortizing loan or where the scheduled balance at the end of the yield maintenance period is included as a deemed final payment. (Equivalently: adding the present value of the scheduled month-48 balance — $14,617,715 ÷ (1 + 4%/12)^18 = $13,767,819 — gives a make-whole of $784,228, which is a different and larger measure than the Term Sheet contemplates.)

**E-2 — What I drafted, and why (Priority 1).** **Section 16.2** implements the Term Sheet's own formulation, which is both faithful to the binding commitment and mathematically determinate: the Yield Maintenance Premium is the greater of (a) **1.00%** of the principal prepaid, and (b) the present value, discounted monthly at the Treasury Rate, of the excess of interest at the **Note rate** over interest at the **Treasury Rate plus 50 basis points**, in each case on the principal prepaid for the remainder of the Yield Maintenance Period, floored at zero. For the same illustrative month-30 prepayment with a 4.00% Treasury rate, the Term Sheet formulation produces **$286,840**, against a 1% floor of $146,177 — so clause (b) governs, as intended. I have also defined the Treasury Rate precisely (H.15 Treasury Constant Maturities, maturity closest to but not exceeding the end of the Yield Maintenance Period, linear interpolation if there is no exact match, determined two Business Days before prepayment), the discounting convention, the zero floor, and Lender's calculation mechanics with a written calculation delivered five Business Days before prepayment.

**E-3 — Where the 50 basis points go changes the number by about $212,000 (Priority 1 — client decision).** You asked me to add the 50 basis points to the **loan rate** and confirm with Marcus. That reading is not what the Term Sheet says: §4.2(b) applies the spread to the *reinvestment* leg ("interest that would accrue … at the treasury rate plus fifty (50) basis points"), which is also the conventional construction. The economic difference is material: on the same illustrative facts, adding 50 bps to the loan rate (your reading) produces **$499,314**, versus **$286,840** under the Term Sheet reading — a difference of **$212,474** on that one prepayment. I have drafted the Term Sheet reading. If Marcus wants your reading, we need his written instruction, and the change should be documented as a negotiated amendment rather than slipped into the draft, because it is a substantive increase in the prepayment cost to Borrower and would be difficult to defend as consistent with the Term Sheet under §14.4.

**E-4 — The 1% floor must survive (Priority 1).** Your draft formula has a zero floor and no minimum. The Term Sheet (§4.2) says "the greater of (a) one percent (1.00%) of the outstanding principal balance … or (b) [the differential]." Deleting the floor would be materially inconsistent with the binding commitment. **Section 16.2(a)** retains it. Note the interaction with **E-2**: because clause (b) is floored at zero and clause (a) is a hard 1%, a Borrower prepaying when Treasury rates have risen still pays 1% — which is the Term Sheet's bargain.

**E-5 — Other prepayment mechanics (Priority 2).** I have drafted: an absolute lockout for months 1–24 (Term Sheet §4.1); whole-loan-only prepayment during the Yield Maintenance Period with 30 days' notice and payment on a Payment Date; partial prepayment in the open period on 15 days' notice, in minimum increments of $500,000 (the increment is an addition — **H-5**); application of partial prepayments to installments of principal in inverse order of maturity without change to the amortization schedule or Maturity Date; and the statement that the premium is bargained-for consideration, not a penalty, with a waiver of the penalty argument (**Section 16.7**). That last provision is drafted to address the enforceability concern you identified: South Carolina courts will enforce a yield maintenance provision that is specific, deterministic and objectively calculable, and the drafting must make that plain on its face.

**E-6 — Casualty and condemnation at par (Priority 2 — client confirmation).** As you asked, I have confirmed the carve-out: **Section 14.4** and **Section 16.5** apply insurance proceeds and condemnation awards to the Indebtedness at par without any premium, and **Section 16.1** preserves that carve-out from the lockout. This is the majority position and I recommend it, but it is not in the Term Sheet; confirm with Marcus.

**E-7 — Premium on acceleration (Priority 3).** **Section 16.6** provides that if Lender accelerates and Borrower tenders the full amount, the Yield Maintenance Premium is due, computed as if the payment were a voluntary prepayment, "to the extent permitted by applicable law." This is lender-favourable and consistent with institutional practice, but its enforceability in South Carolina after Lender's own acceleration is not free from doubt. The savings language is deliberate. Borrower's counsel will negotiate it; I would not concede it, but we should not rely on it in the credit decision.

## G. COVENANT, DEFAULT AND GUARANTY ISSUES

**G-1 — Net worth and liquidity: the Term Sheet and your note disagree on the obligor (Priority 1 — client decision).** Term Sheet §7.2 imposes the $1,000,000 net worth and $500,000 liquidity covenants on **Borrower** ("Borrower shall maintain at all times during the term of the Loan"). Your §6 note attributes them to **Guarantor**. These are very different credit propositions: a $1,000,000 net worth covenant applied to Borrower is a working-capital test; applied to Guarantor — whose net worth is stated in Term Sheet §1.3 at approximately $28,000,000 — it is nearly meaningless, because compliance is a 28-to-1 cushion. **Section 7.8(b)** implements the Term Sheet (Borrower) and **Section 7.8(c)** imposes the same thresholds on Guarantor as an addition, with **Section 12.1(b)** making a Guarantor breach a default. Neither threshold is appropriate in my view: I recommend (i) confirming with Marcus which obligor he intends; and (ii) if Guarantor, raising the thresholds substantially (for example a floor tied to a percentage of the outstanding principal balance, with a covenant not to permit net worth to fall below a stated level and liquidity of at least 5% of the Loan), consistent with the $28,000,000 starting point. The interaction is workable but inelegant; if the client wants the two periods aligned, we can conform both to 10 calendar days. ## E. PREPAYMENT AND YIELD MAINTENANCE ISSUES

**E-1 — The formula in the Markup Notes produces a zero premium; I have drafted a different formula (Priority 1).** Your §5 draft provides that the premium equals the positive excess of "(A) the present value of all remaining scheduled monthly payments of interest and principal from the prepayment date through the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period … over (B) the outstanding principal amount being prepaid," floored at zero. Applied to this Loan, the result is not a small premium — it is a large negative number:

| Element (illustrative prepayment at month 30; 18 months remaining; 25-year amortization) | Amount |
|:---|---:|
| Outstanding principal at month 30 | $14,617,715 |
| Present value of the 18 remaining scheduled P&I installments, discounted at a 4.00% Treasury rate | $1,634,124 |
| Excess of (A) over (B) | **$(12,983,591)** — i.e. zero premium |

The defect is structural, not arithmetical: with 25-year amortization and a 60-month maturity, **there is no scheduled balloon payment at the end of the Yield Maintenance Period**, so the stream of "remaining scheduled monthly payments" never includes repayment of principal. A formula of this kind works only for a fully amortizing loan or where the scheduled balance at the end of the yield maintenance period is included as a deemed final payment. (Equivalently: adding the present value of the scheduled month-48 balance — $14,617,715 ÷ (1 + 4%/12)^18 = $13,767,819 — gives a make-whole of $784,228, which is a different and larger measure than the Term Sheet contemplates.)

**E-2 — What I drafted, and why (Priority 1).** **Section 16.2** implements the Term Sheet's own formulation, which is both faithful to the binding commitment and mathematically determinate: the Yield Maintenance Premium is the greater of (a) **1.00%** of the principal prepaid, and (b) the present value, discounted monthly at the Treasury Rate, of the excess of interest at the **Note rate** over interest at the **Treasury Rate plus 50 basis points**, in each case on the principal prepaid for the remainder of the Yield Maintenance Period, floored at zero. For the same illustrative month-30 prepayment with a 4.00% Treasury rate, the Term Sheet formulation produces **$286,840**, against a 1% floor of $146,177 — so clause (b) governs, as intended. I have also defined the Treasury Rate precisely (H.15 Treasury Constant Maturities, maturity closest to but not exceeding the end of the Yield Maintenance Period, linear interpolation if there is no exact match, determined two Business Days before prepayment), the discounting convention, the zero floor, and Lender's calculation mechanics with a written calculation delivered five Business Days before prepayment.

**E-3 — Where the 50 basis points go changes the number by about $212,000 (Priority 1 — client decision).** You asked me to add the 50 basis points to the **loan rate** and confirm with Marcus. That reading is not what the Term Sheet says: §4.2(b) applies the spread to the *reinvestment* leg ("interest that would accrue … at the treasury rate plus fifty (50) basis points"), which is also the conventional construction. The economic difference is material: on the same illustrative facts, adding 50 bps to the loan rate (your reading) produces **$499,314**, versus **$286,840** under the Term Sheet reading — a difference of **$212,474** on that one prepayment. I have drafted the Term Sheet reading. If Marcus wants your reading, we need his written instruction, and the change should be documented as a negotiated amendment rather than slipped into the draft, because it is a substantive increase in the prepayment cost to Borrower and would be difficult to defend as consistent with the Term Sheet under §14.4.

**E-4 — The 1% floor must survive (Priority 1).** Your draft formula has a zero floor and no minimum. The Term Sheet (§4.2) says "the greater of (a) one percent (1.00%) of the outstanding principal balance … or (b) [the differential]." Deleting the floor would be materially inconsistent with the binding commitment. **Section 16.2(a)** retains it. Note the interaction with **E-2**: because clause (b) is floored at zero and clause (a) is a hard 1%, a Borrower prepaying when Treasury rates have risen still pays 1% — which is the Term Sheet's bargain.

**E-5 — Other prepayment mechanics (Priority 2).** I have drafted: an absolute lockout for months 1–24 (Term Sheet §4.1); whole-loan-only prepayment during the Yield Maintenance Period with 30 days' notice and payment on a Payment Date; partial prepayment in the open period on 15 days' notice, in minimum increments of $500,000 (the increment is an addition — **H-5**); application of partial prepayments to installments of principal in inverse order of maturity without change to the amortization schedule or Maturity Date; and the statement that the premium is bargained-for consideration, not a penalty, with a waiver of the penalty argument (**Section 16.7**). That last provision is drafted to address the enforceability concern you identified: South Carolina courts will enforce a yield maintenance provision that is specific, deterministic and objectively calculable, and the drafting must make that plain on its face.

**E-6 — Casualty and condemnation at par (Priority 2 — client confirmation).** As you asked, I have confirmed the carve-out: **Section 14.4** and **Section 16.5** apply insurance proceeds and condemnation awards to the Indebtedness at par without any premium, and **Section 16.1** preserves that carve-out from the lockout. This is the majority position and I recommend it, but it is not in the Term Sheet; confirm with Marcus.

**E-7 — Premium on acceleration (Priority 3).** **Section 16.6** provides that if Lender accelerates and Borrower tenders the full amount, the Yield Maintenance Premium is due, computed as if the payment were a voluntary prepayment, "to the extent permitted by applicable law." This is lender-favourable and consistent with institutional practice, but its enforceability in South Carolina after Lender's own acceleration is not free from doubt. The savings language is deliberate. Borrower's counsel will negotiate it; I would not concede it, but we should not rely on it in the credit decision.

## F. LEASES, RENTS AND TENANT ISSUES

**F-1 — Lowcountry Provisions: no assignment, estoppel or SNDA provision (Priority 1).** The lease abstract states flatly: "Assignment/Subletting: **No provision.** Lease is silent on assignment or subletting rights and does not contain a consent requirement, prohibition, or landlord approval mechanism," and "Estoppel Certificate Obligation: Lease does not contain a provision requiring tenant to deliver estoppel certificates," and "SNDA: Lease does not contain SNDA provisions." The appraiser independently flags the omission as "unusual for a lease of this type." Your three-step best practice is implemented at **Section 5.2(e)** (representation of authority to assign, naming the lease), **Section 5.6** (estoppel and SNDA delivery obligation with the closing condition) and **Section 5.6(ii)** (post-closing covenant to obtain a conforming amendment at the next renewal, extension or amendment, outside date March 31, 2027). Two caveats: the estoppel is not obtainable as of right (**B-9**), and the statutory citation used in the draft needs verification (**F-2**).

**F-2 — Statutory citation for the assignment of rents requires verification (Priority 2).** Your note cites the South Carolina Uniform Assignment of Rents Act as "S.C. Code § 29-3-100 *et seq.*" I have drafted the instrument to cite "the South Carolina Uniform Assignment of Rents Act, Chapter 3, Title 29 of the South Carolina Code of Laws, as amended," without a pinpoint section range, because the pinpoint in the file does not match the codification as I understand it and a recorded instrument should not carry an incorrect citation. *Action:* confirm the current section range and the Act's enforcement and notice mechanics before the Mortgage is executed; if the Act's notice provisions impose requirements beyond "written notice to the tenants" (**Section 5.4**), conform the drafting. This is a short research task and I will complete it this week.

**F-3 — Absolute versus collateral assignment: characterization risk (Priority 2).** I have implemented your instruction to restyle the assignment as absolute and present and to remove all "collateral" language (**Article 5**). I should record one consequence for the file: in a Borrower bankruptcy, an "absolute" assignment of rents is frequently recharacterized as a security interest, in which case the rents become cash collateral subject to the automatic stay and the Lender's entitlement to collect may be contested. The revocable license in **Section 5.3** and the notice mechanics in **Section 5.4** preserve the practical benefit, and the absolute form is better than the collateral form against third parties and in state-court enforcement. The recommendation stands; this note is for the file so that the client is not surprised if the issue arises.

**F-4 — Harmon & Wren: right of first refusal, renewal timing and the renovation overlap (Priority 2).** Three interacting problems. (i) The tenant holds a **ROFR on Bay 2** exercisable within 15 business days of a bona fide third-party offer, and it **survives renewal** of the Bay 3 lease; any Bay 2 lease must therefore be sequenced around it. (ii) The Bay 3 lease expires **June 30, 2026** with a renewal notice deadline of **December 31, 2025** — 15 days after the Substantial Completion Deadline of June 15, 2026 expires, and the renewal decision falls in the middle of the renovation, when the tenant is experiencing the most disruption and has the strongest argument to leave. (iii) The tenant's early-termination right (3 months' rent, effective June 30, 2025) lapsed unexercised because the December 31, 2024 notice deadline passed — that is a favourable fact and should be recorded in the estoppel. **Section 7.3** requires Lender consent for leases over 5,000 SF or over 5 years (so the 3,800 SF Bay 2 lease and the 3-year renewal do not require consent), and the continuation paragraph of **Section 7.3** requires Mortgagor to obtain Lender approval of the material terms of any proposed Bay 2 third-party lease *before* presenting it to Harmon & Wren, so that we do not find ourselves approving a lease that the ROFR mechanics then change. *Action:* diarise the December 31, 2025 renewal deadline; require the estoppel to confirm the ROFR terms, the lapsed termination right and the renewal option.

**F-5 — Security deposits (Priority 3).** Deposits total **$69,183** (Lowcountry $18,050; Harmon & Wren $15,200; Tidemark $35,933), each equal to two months' base rent. **Section 5.7** makes clear that the deposits remain the tenants' property, that the Lien attaches only to Mortgagor's interest, and that Mortgagor must account for and transfer them on demand. I have deliberately not treated them as free collateral; doing so would create lender liability at the moment of enforcement.

**F-6 — Tidemark's assignment consent is at the landlord's sole discretion (Priority 3).** The Tidemark lease permits assignment only with the landlord's consent "which may be withheld in Landlord's sole discretion" and subletting with consent not to be unreasonably withheld. This matters for the maturity rollover (**A-8**) and if the Lender ever takes title through foreclosure: a tenant whose consent standard is favourable to the landlord may resist attornment, and the SNDA the lease requires (**Section 5.6**) should be obtained in the Lender's standard form, not the tenant's.

## G. COVENANT, DEFAULT AND GUARANTY ISSUES

**G-1 — Net worth and liquidity: the Term Sheet and your note disagree on the obligor (Priority 1 — client decision).** Term Sheet §7.2 imposes the $1,000,000 net worth and $500,000 liquidity covenants on **Borrower** ("Borrower shall maintain at all times during the term of the Loan"). Your §6 note attributes them to **Guarantor**. These are very different credit propositions: a $1,000,000 net worth covenant applied to Borrower is a working-capital test; applied to Guarantor — whose net worth is stated in Term Sheet §1.3 at approximately $28,000,000 — it is nearly meaningless, because compliance is a 28-to-1 cushion. **Section 7.8(b)** implements the Term Sheet (Borrower) and **Section 7.8(c)** imposes the same thresholds on Guarantor as an addition, with **Section 12.1(b)** making a Guarantor breach a default. Neither threshold is appropriate in my view: I recommend (i) confirming with Marcus which obligor he intends; and (ii) if Guarantor, raising the thresholds substantially (for example a floor tied to a percentage of the outstanding principal balance, with a covenant not to permit net worth to fall below a stated level and liquidity of at least 5% of the Loan), consistent with the $28,000,000 starting point. As drafted, the instrument is defensible but toothless on this point.

**G-2 — The Term Sheet's cure provisions do not cover insurance defaults (Priority 2).** Section 11.2(b) of the Term Sheet grants a 30/90-day cure to non-monetary defaults "other than SPE defaults, transfer restriction defaults, and insurance defaults," but Section 11.2(c) grants "no cure period" only to SPE and transfer defaults. Insurance defaults therefore fall into a gap: excluded from the cure in (b), not picked up by (c). **Section 12.2(b)** and **Section 12.2(c)(vi)** resolve it by treating insurance defaults as having no cure period, which is the only reading consistent with the exclusion. Flagging it because Borrower's counsel will notice, and because a 30-day cure for a lapse in coverage is arguably what the Term Sheet intended.

**G-3 — The DSCR default has no cure mechanism (Priority 1).** Section 11.1(i) of the Term Sheet makes two consecutive quarters below 1.25x a default "without cure," and Section 11.2 provides no cure. **Section 12.1(i)** and **Section 12.2** follow. Combined with **A-2** (the covenant cannot be met), the Loan is in structural default from the first test date unless lease-up dramatically outperforms the borrower's own projections. Recommend the client adopt either a DSCR cure deposit (Borrower deposits the shortfall into a lender-held reserve, which cures the default), a cash sweep above a 1.10x threshold, or an additional guaranty, and that we draft the corresponding credit support before the instrument is executed rather than after.

**G-4 — Late charge and payment cure interact awkwardly (Priority 3).** The Late Charge accrues if an installment is not received within **10 calendar days** (Term Sheet §3.11; **Section 15.4**), while the payment default cure period is **5 Business Days** (Term Sheet §11.2(a); **Section 12.2(a)**). A payment received on day 7 or 8 is in default (cure expired) but incurs no late charge; a payment received on day 9 or 10 is in default and incurs a late charge. **Section 12.2(a)** notes that the Late Charge may be assessed independently and does not extend the cure period. The interaction is workable but inelegant; if the client wants the two periods aligned, we can conform both to 10 calendar days. Separately, a 5% late charge is at the upper end of what South Carolina courts are likely to enforce as a reasonable estimate of administrative cost, and **Section 15.4** includes the recitals (difficulty of ascertainment, reasonable estimate, not a penalty) intended to support enforceability; **Section 15.8** provides an interest-rate savings clause. I would not expect difficulty at 5% but the recitals should stay.

**G-5 — Default rate of 10.85% (Priority 3).** Applicable Rate 5.85% plus 5.00% = **10.85%**. **Section 15.8** contains a full interest-rate limitation and savings provision, which I recommend retaining regardless: it protects against the risk that the Default Rate (which continues during the pendency of a bankruptcy) or the combination of default interest and late charges is held to exceed an applicable ceiling. I have not opined on the South Carolina usury ceiling in this memorandum; a short confirmation against S.C. Code Ann. Title 34, Chapter 31 should be added to the research list alongside **F-2**.

**G-6 — "Full recourse personal guaranty" is a misdescription (Priority 2).** Term Sheet §5.5 is headed "**Guaranty**" and opens with the statement that Guarantor "shall execute and deliver a full recourse personal guaranty," then immediately structures it as (a) a non-recourse carve-out guaranty, (b) a completion guaranty and (c) an interest-shortfall guaranty limited to 14 months. Only the carve-out limb is "full recourse," and only on a bad-boy event; the rest is limited. The Mortgage reflects the actual structure (**Section 18.14**, **Section 7.18**) rather than the heading. This matters for credit: the personal guaranty does not support debt service generally, so the lender's real protection is the Property, the completion guaranty and a 14-month interest backstop against an 81% as-is LTV and a covenant that cannot be met.

**G-7 — The completion guaranty needs a cost-of-completion mechanism (Priority 2).** Term Sheet §5.5(b) guarantees completion "within the approved renovation budget and by the Substantial Completion Deadline." The Mortgage cross-references it (**Section 10.6**, **Section 7.18**) and gives Lender the right to complete the Project and charge the cost (**Section 10.10**). *Action:* confirm that the Completion Guaranty, when delivered, covers budget overruns as well as physical completion, and that it is not discharged by Lender's own completion (a common carve-out in guarantor-favourable forms).

**G-8 — The ten-month unguarded gap (Priority 1).** The payment guaranty covers an interest shortfall for the first 14 months. Substantial Completion is due at month 14. The first DSCR test is at month 24. Between month 15 and month 24 there is neither a guaranty of debt service nor a tested covenant — and, on the borrower's own projections, that is the period in which Suite B is only just commencing rent (projected February 1, 2027, which is 2.5 months before the April 15, 2027 test date the borrower assumes). Recommend to Marcus that the interest-shortfall guaranty be extended through at least the first DSCR test date (and preferably through the earlier of stabilization or month 36), and that a DSCR/interest reserve be funded at closing from the equity contribution — which, per **A-4**, also has no source at present.

## H. DOCUMENTATION, CLOSING AND DRAFTING ADDITIONS

**H-1 — The Note, the Guaranty and the GC Contract are not in the file (Priority 1).** The Mortgage states the Loan's terms (principal $14,750,000; Applicable Rate of Daily SOFR + 2.85% subject to a 3.00% SOFR floor, i.e. a 5.85% all-in floor; interest-only months 1–24; 25-year amortization from month 25; payments on the 15th commencing May 15, 2025; Maturity Date April 15, 2030) subject to the Note in the event of conflict (**Section 15.1**). Those terms come from the Term Sheet, not from the Note, which has not been produced. *Action:* obtain the Note and conform every figure; obtain the Guaranty, Completion Guaranty and Environmental Indemnity Agreements and confirm that the Mortgage's cross-references (Articles 12, 17 and 18.14) match their defined terms and carve-outs. The GC Contract is likewise referenced (defined term "GC Contract"; **Section 6.13**) but not produced; the executed copy is a Term Sheet closing condition (§12.1(l)) and is needed to add the environmental covenant required by **C-2**.

**H-2 — Interest computation convention is not specified in the Term Sheet (Priority 2).** The Term Sheet says only that interest accrues at Daily SOFR plus 2.85%, without specifying the day-count or compounding convention. **Section 15.2** adopts **actual/360**, which is conventional for SOFR-based commercial loans and produces a marginally higher effective rate than actual/365 (by a factor of 365/360, or about 1.39%). This is a real economic term to which Borrower's counsel will object if they are alert. *Action:* confirm with Marcus before execution; if he prefers actual/365 or a compounded-in-arrears convention, **Section 15.2** and the Note must be conformed together.

**H-3 — Benchmark replacement provision added (Priority 2).** Nothing in the Term Sheet addresses the cessation or unavailability of Daily SOFR. **Section 15.11** adds a customary benchmark replacement mechanism (successor rate plus spread adjustment, conforming changes, amendment mechanics with a 15-day notice and a lender-unilateral fallback if Borrower does not execute). This is an addition (**H-5**) but a necessary one: without it the Note would have no mechanism if Daily SOFR is discontinued, and the loan would be unadministrable.

**H-4 — Insurance: cost consequences of the Lender's requirements (Priority 3).** The draft implements the Term Sheet amounts — all-risk at replacement cost with agreed amount, CGL $2,000,000/$5,000,000, flood **$5,000,000** in FEMA Zone X, builder's risk $3,150,000, workers' compensation, and umbrella $5,000,000, all with A-:VII carriers and 30 days' notice (**Article 8**). Two observations: the $5,000,000 flood requirement in Zone X is a Lender-imposed condition and will be a real cost (and possibly hard to place at that limit in Zone X, where carriers may question the exposure); and builder's risk at the full $3,150,000 budget is higher than the GC contract sum ($2,850,000) because it must cover the soft costs and contingency — that is correct as drafted and should not be reduced to the contract sum. I added **business income/rent loss insurance of 12 months (Section 8.1(g))**, which the Term Sheet does not require; given the 56.13% occupancy and the debt service coverage shortfall, rent loss coverage matters more here than usual.

**H-5 — Additions to the Term Sheet, for the client's approval (Priority 2).** Section 14.4 of the Term Sheet permits Lender to require additional provisions "consistent with Lender's customary documentation requirements and applicable law" and not "materially inconsistent with the terms of this Term Sheet." The following additions in the draft should be identified to Marcus so that they are approved rather than discovered: (i) pro-rata lender/equity funding test for Draws (**Section 10.2(d)**); (ii) change-order approval thresholds of $50,000 each / $100,000 aggregate (**Section 7.7(d)**); (iii) the indirect and upstream change-of-control restrictions (**Section 7.5(c)**); (iv) additional "actual loss" carve-outs in **Section 18.14(f)** (insurance, waste, taxes, failure to deliver Rents, litigation costs); (v) business income and rent loss insurance (**Section 8.1(g)**); (vi) partial prepayment minimum increments of $500,000 (**Section 16.4**); (vii) benchmark replacement (**Section 15.11**); (viii) the $250,000 thresholds for settling insurance and condemnation claims (**Section 14.1**) and for judgment and cross-default Events of Default (**Sections 12.1(e), 12.1(p)**); (ix) the minimum $1,000,000/​$500,000 covenants applied additionally to Guarantor (**Section 7.8(c)**); (x) the requirement that undisbursed holdback be applied to principal or retained after Substantial Completion rather than released (**Section 10.11**); and (xi) the express denial of Borrower's right to partial prepayment during the Yield Maintenance Period (Term Sheet consistent, but stated as an absolute). Items (iv) and (x) are the ones Borrower's counsel is most likely to resist and the ones with the greatest real economic content.

**H-6 — Conditions precedent and closing checklist (Priority 2).** Section 12.1 of the Term Sheet lists fourteen conditions precedent plus a catch-all. For the closing checklist, note that several are not yet evidenced in the file: satisfactory evidence of the $6,200,000 equity contribution (§12.1(m)) — see **A-4**; the executed construction contract with all amendments (§12.1(l)); estoppels and SNDAs from all three tenants (§12.1(j)–(k)) — see **B-9**; legal opinions (§12.1(h)) — we will need Borrower's counsel to opine on organisational matters, authority and enforceability, and the enforceability opinion depends on receiving the full operating agreement (**D-8**); insurance certificates (§12.1(f)); and good standing certificates (§12.1(g)). I will build the closing checklist from Section 12.1 plus the requirements in Schedule B-I of the Title Commitment and the additional items flagged in this memorandum.

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `mortgage-and-security-agreement.docx` | 70-page first draft of the South Carolina Mortgage and Security Agreement (with absolute assignment of leases, rents, issues and profits) from Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC to Calverley Heritage Bank, Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047, for 520–534 King Street, Charleston, SC. |
| `drafting-issues-memorandum.docx` | 31-page privileged issues memorandum from the drafting associate to the supervising partner, responding to the March 18 markup notes and cataloguing every cross-document inconsistency, recomputed figure and open item. |

## What the mortgage contains

Drafted to the executed Term Sheet of April 1, 2025 and the Title Commitment, organised as Articles 1–18 plus Exhibits A–E:

- **Granting clause** covering all three tax parcels and the vacated Anson Lane strip, with the full collateral schedule (fixtures, FF&E, accounts, proceeds, permits, contracts including the GC contract, leases and rents).
- **Article 5 — absolute and present assignment of rents** restyled from a collateral assignment, with a revocable licence to collect, enforcement on written notice to tenants, and the Lowcountry Provisions remediation covenant.
- **Article 7.4 — full single-purpose entity and separateness covenants**, including the independent-manager bankruptcy consent, and **7.5** direct *and* indirect/upstream transfer restrictions.
- **Article 7.6 + Exhibit E — specific SCDHEC land use restriction covenants** (no residential use of the Bay 1 ground floor; vapour barrier maintenance; no penetration without SCDHEC approval; annual certification) with a dedicated, uncurable Event of Default.
- **Article 10 — renovation holdback** of $2,250,000 against a $3,150,000 budget: draw conditions, AIA certifications, lien waivers, title date-downs, 10% retainage, equity-funding ratio test, June 15, 2026 substantial completion deadline.
- **Article 16 — prepayment** with an absolute 24-month lockout, a self-contained yield maintenance formula (greater of 1% or the present value of the interest differential, Treasury Rate defined and interpolated), and open prepayment in months 49–60.
- **Articles 12–13 — defaults and remedies**, stated expressly as judicial foreclosure only with no power of sale, plus receivership as of right.
- **Exhibits** — A legal description, B permitted exceptions, C budget and draw schedule, D rent roll and lease provisions, E land use restriction compliance protocol.

## Principal findings in the memorandum

The review recomputed 39 figures and identified 16 cross-document conflicts. The largest:

1. **The DSCR covenant cannot be met.** On the borrower's own stabilised projections, NOI of $622,772 supports 0.72x on interest-only debt service and 0.55x on amortising debt service against a 1.25x covenant tested from month 24 — the same month amortisation starts. A 1.25x test would support roughly a $6.5m loan.
2. **Occupancy is 56.13%, not 68%.** The Term Sheet and appraisal both use 21,400 occupied SF where the rent roll supports 17,400; the Term Sheet's own two occupancy statements contradict each other.
3. **Sources and uses do not balance** — loan plus equity equals project cost exactly, leaving at least $352,075 of closing costs and the $150,000 TI/LC reserve unfunded.
4. **The proposed yield maintenance formula produces a zero premium** for a partially amortising loan (no scheduled balloon at month 48), and dropping the 1% floor would conflict with the binding Term Sheet; placement of the 50 bps changes the premium by ~$212,000.
5. **The operating agreement does not support the SPE structure** — no independent manager, no separateness covenants, and bankruptcy is not a "Major Decision", so the 72% managing member could file the borrower unilaterally.
6. **Anson Lane derives from a quitclaim deed** with the Title Insurer expressly disclaiming that its chain matches Parcel One; affirmative coverage must be confirmed and endorsed.
7. **A ten-month guaranty gap** — the interest-shortfall guaranty ends at month 14, DSCR testing begins at month 24.

Every memorandum risk is tied to a numbered body issue (A-1 to H-6), and each to the specific mortgage provision that addresses it, with 19 open information requests, 20 recorded drafting decisions, and an arithmetic verification log.

## Verification performed

Figures were recomputed independently in Python (debt service, DSCR, LTV/LTC, occupancy, holdback allocations, draw schedule totals, mortgage recording tax, capital reserve, security deposits, balloon balance, prepayment illustrations). Internal cross-references were machine-checked across both documents. Both .docx files pass ECMA-376 schema validation, render without text overflow at the margins, and were proof-checked from a PDF render.
"}

Articles 1–18 plus Exhibits A–E: granting clause covering all three tax parcels and the vacated Anson Lane strip; UCC fixture filing; future-advance/priority provisions for the $2,250,000 holdback; absolute (not collateral) assignment of rents with a revocable licence and tenant-notice enforcement; full SPE/separateness covenants incl. independent-manager bankruptcy consent; specific SCDHEC land use restriction covenants (no residential use of Bay 1, vapour barrier maintenance, SCDHEC notice, annual certification) with an uncurable Event of Default; draw procedures with lien waivers, title date-downs and 10% retainage; insurance; escrows/reserves; precise, self-contained yield maintenance formula; judicial-foreclosure-only remedies (expressly no power of sale); non-recourse carve-outs; signature and notarial blocks.

**2. `drafting-issues-memorandum.docx`** — a 31-page privileged memorandum to the supervising partner responding section-by-section to her markup notes and flagging every departure. Contains a 12-item priority risk register, 56 numbered issues (A-1 to H-6) each tied to the mortgage provision that addresses it, 20 recorded drafting decisions, a 39-figure arithmetic verification log, 16 catalogued cross-document conflicts, 19 open information requests and a dated timetable.

Key findings documented: the 1.25x DSCR covenant is unachievable (0.72x interest-only / 0.55x amortising even at the borrower's stabilised case); occupancy is 56.13% not 68%; sources and uses leave at least $352,075 unfunded; the proposed yield maintenance formula in the markup notes produces a zero premium and conflicts with the Term Sheet's 1% floor; the operating agreement lacks every required SPE provision and leaves bankruptcy outside the 75% "Major Decisions" list; Anson Lane derives from a quitclaim deed with disclaimed chain equivalence; and the interest-shortfall guaranty leaves months 15–24 unguarded.
